label: Review of Tensors
notes: This appendix spans printed pages 391 through 406 and gathers the algebra of tensors that every later chapter assumes. We treat multilinear maps, the tensor product, covariant and contravariant types, tensor bundles and fields, symmetry, the wedge product, the exterior derivative, and contraction in one compact pass.

label: Multilinear Maps
notes: A multilinear map is linear in each slot when the others are frozen. The bilinear case is the workhorse: feeding two vectors returns a scalar that respects scaling and addition separately in each argument. This separate-linearity is the structural fingerprint that distinguishes tensors from ordinary linear maps.

label: The Tensor Product
notes: The tensor product packages a multilinear map as a single linear object on a larger space. Its universal property says every multilinear map factors uniquely through the canonical map into the tensor product, so building tensors and proving identities reduces to checking statements on simple decomposable elements.

label: Covariant and Contravariant Tensors
notes: A tensor of a given type takes copies of the tangent space and copies of its dual. Covariant slots eat vectors and lower indices, contravariant slots eat covectors and raise them. The metric is the canonical covariant two-tensor and its inverse is the contravariant partner.

label: The Tensor Bundle
notes: Assembling all tensors of a fixed type over every point of the manifold yields the tensor bundle, a smooth vector bundle whose fiber is the tensor space at that point. Local frames and coframes produce coordinate components, and transition functions act by the appropriate tensor power of the Jacobian.

label: Tensor Fields
notes: A tensor field is a smooth section of a tensor bundle: a tensor chosen at each point that varies smoothly. In coordinates it is a smoothly varying array of component functions. Smoothness can be tested either by component functions or by feeding the field smooth vector and covector arguments.

label: Symmetric and Alternating Tensors
notes: Covariant tensors split by their behavior under permuting arguments. Symmetric tensors are unchanged by swaps and carry quadratic forms like the metric. Alternating tensors flip sign under a transposition and vanish on repeated arguments, which is exactly the structure that measures oriented volume of parallelepipeds.

label: The Wedge Product
notes: The wedge product antisymmetrizes the tensor product, producing alternating tensors that are graded-commutative. Two covectors wedged together build the oriented area element of the parallelogram they span, and the determinant appears naturally as the coefficient relating wedge products of basis covectors across a change of frame.

label: Differential Forms
notes: A differential k-form is an alternating covariant k-tensor field. The forms of all degrees assemble into the exterior algebra bundle, and a one-form pairs with vectors to return functions. Forms are precisely the objects that can be integrated over oriented submanifolds, which motivates the entire calculus that follows.

label: The Exterior Derivative
notes: The exterior derivative raises form degree by one, generalizes the differential of a function, and squares to zero. It is the unique antiderivation extending the gradient that is natural under pullback. The identity d composed with d equals zero encodes that mixed partials commute and underlies de Rham cohomology.

label: Tensor Contraction and Index Notation
notes: Contraction pairs one contravariant slot with one covariant slot and sums, lowering type by one in each. In index notation a repeated upper and lower index is summed by the Einstein convention. The trace of an endomorphism and the divergence of a tensor field are the most familiar contractions in practice.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: We assembled the full tensor toolkit: multilinear maps, the tensor product, covariant and contravariant types, bundles and fields, symmetry, the wedge product, differential forms, the exterior derivative, and contraction. Every Riemannian construction ahead, from the metric to curvature, is expressed in exactly this language, so fluency here pays off repeatedly.
